papers.title: Geodesics and a Hubble Relation in Nonstationary Thermodynamic Geometry
papers.abstract: Thermodynamic geometry offers a versatile lens from equilibrium to nonequilibrium, yet typically assumes a stationary metric. Here we study nonstationary thermodynamic geometry, where the metric evolves even at fixed control parameters. The resulting temporal connection generalizes the geodesic equation and redistributes dissipation along optimal control paths. We further establish a thermodynamic Hubble relation that distinguishes relaxation toward equilibrium from geometric expansion or contraction. Brownian examples demonstrate that externally modulated friction can reduce minimum dissipation, while heat exchange with a finite reservoir can induce geometric contraction and Mpemba-type relaxation. Our framework lays a geometric foundation for understanding complex evolving nonequilibrium systems.

papers.title: Field-Driven Active Matter Physics and Material Applications
papers.abstract: Active matter consists of energy-consuming units that generate motion, making it a powerful platform for exploring nonequilibrium physics and engineering adaptive materials. Robotic active matter brings this physics into programmable, macroscopic agents with controllable actuation, sensing, and response, but its scalability is limited by onboard power, communication, and control complexity. Field-driven active matter addresses these limitations by shifting part of the control burden from individual agents to external or environmental fields, such as magnetic, electric, acoustic, optical, and fluidic fields, which can power, guide, and couple many agents simultaneously. Beyond applications in targeted navigation, adaptive collaboration, and flexible transport, field-driven robotic active matter offers a controllable testbed for nonequilibrium phenomena that are difficult to isolate in molecular or colloidal active matter, including tunable interactions, programmable phase transitions, solid-fluid switching, hyperuniform order, and reconfigurable collective motion. Here, we present field-driven active matter as a bridge between active matter physics and functional material engineering, organized through a unified field-to-information-to-physics-to-function framework that links field-mediated interactions, information processing, and memory to collective transport, reconfiguration, and mechanical performance. By distributing control between agents and fields, field-driven active matter offers a pathway toward intelligent materials capable of sensing, adaptation, computation, reconfiguration, and performing complex tasks, while expanding both the scientific scope of nonequilibrium physics and the practical capabilities of engineered matter.

papers.title: A Beginner's Guide to Physical Networks
papers.abstract: Network theory studies entities (nodes) and the relationships between them (edges). While these entities and their relationships may be abstract in general, this tutorial focuses on the special case of physical networks: spatially embedded networks that carry physical quantities such as electric charge, fluid volume, or momentum. The underlying structure is described mathematically by a graph (Section I), with the incidence matrix playing a central role in the analysis. Viewing a graph as a special case of a cell complex reveals the topological structure of the incidence matrix and its relation to familiar operators from calculus (Section II). Because these networks are physical, flows are conserved at each node and often derive from the gradient of a potential. Models that satisfy these principles behave analogously to circuits; accordingly, we first review circuit theory (Section III), then examine related fluid flow (Section IV) and mechanical (Section V) networks. Briefly, the topics of random walkers (Section VI) and nonlinear networks (Section VII) will be discussed, followed by concluding remarks (Section VIII). Analytical examples and Python implementations, in lieu of pseudocode, are included throughout. Exercises are included as footnotes. This tutorial is based on a short course taught at the Boulder School for Condensed Matter in 2019 and a course taught at the University of Pennsylvania in Spring 2024. It should be a useful resource for students, teachers, and researchers applying graph theory to physical networks. Knowledge of linear algebra is assumed, but no prior knowledge of graph theory or physics is necessary.

papers.title: Revisiting Stress Analysis in a Three-Dimensional Elastic Hollow Sphere under Uniaxial Compression via the Inverse Laplace Transform Expressions within an Elastodynamic Framework
papers.abstract: The stress analysis of a three-dimensional elastic hollow sphere subjected to uniaxial compression is revisited, employing an elastodynamic framework. Through the application of the Laplace transform, the scalar and vector potentials of displacement are expanded, facilitating a detailed exploration of the system's mechanical behavior. The static solutions for displacement and stress distributions are derived in the long-time limit, which reveal key insights into the response of the elastic hollow sphere. Notably, on the inner surface, certain quantities exhibit a peak at the point where the angle between the compressive force and the point on the surface becomes perpendicular, indicating localized stress concentration. These findings provide a robust analytical approach for understanding and predicting the behavior of elastic hollow spheres under uniaxial loading, with implications for material science and structural engineering.

papers.title: Geometry-Derived Capacitance Dyadics with Floquet Sideband Correction for Anisotropic Periodic Patch Metasurfaces
papers.abstract: Homogenised sheet models describe periodic metallic patch layers using a scalar sheet capacitance, which is only valid when the effective response is isotropic. An isotropic response exists for unit cells with patch geometries that have rotational symmetry of order three or higher. Lower-symmetry unit cells with irregular or random geometries generically require a full 2 x 2 surface-capacitance dyadic. We present a framework that computes this dyadic directly from the arbitrary gap-connected patch geometry on a unit cell of a hexagonal lattice. The two-dimensional Bravais periodicity fixes the two independent macroscopic loading directions, the connectivity of the gap ensures a full-rank response for the geometries considered here, and the point-group symmetry of the patch constrains the form of the dyadic. A quasi-static boundary value problem on a single periodic cell then determines its independent entries. We use the surface-capacitance dyadic in the anisotropic surface- wave dispersion relation, which includes the leading spatially-dispersive first shell Floquet-sideband correction. For each new patch geometry, the dyadic and the first-shell correction are obtained from a single quasi-static cell problem and from the reconstructed boundary. So anisotropic surface- wave dispersion follows without a per-geometry full-wave eigenmode band sweep or sheet-tensor retrieval. We validate this geometry-to-dispersion chain against full-wave eigenmode simulations across six representative symmetry classes, showing that the correction captures band flattening near the Brillouin-zone boundary and improves agreement relative to the local dyadic model.

papers.title: The magnetic field of a homogeneously magnetized circular piece
papers.abstract: The magnetic field of a homogeneously magnetized circular piece, i.e. the part of a finite cylinder that is cut off by two planes parallel to the coordinate axes, is determined. The field is expressed as the product between the demagnetization tensor describing the geometrical part of the problem and the magnetization. All nine components of the tensor are expressed in closed form in terms of elementary functions and incomplete elliptic integrals of the first, second and third kind. The complementary geometrical piece, bounded by the same arc from the outside, is obtained from the same expressions. The solution, implemented in the open source magnetic framework MagTense, is verified against direct numerical integration and against a finite element calculation of the magnetic field, showing excellent agreement.

papers.title: The magnetic field of a homogeneously magnetized cone
papers.abstract: The magnetic field of a homogeneously magnetized right circular cone is determined. The field is expressed as the product between the demagnetization tensor describing the geometrical part of the problem and the magnetization. Additionally, its magnetic scalar potential is expressed as the product between a demagnetization vector and the magnetization. All nine components of the tensor and three components of the vector are expressed in terms of elliptic integrals of the first, second and third kind, and a single scalar function of the field point. This function is given as a one-dimensional integral and as a series, and it reduces to the known logarithm on the axis of the cone. The demagnetization tensor and vector for the truncated cone and the annular cone are given by simple superposition. The magnetometric demagnetization tensor is also derived in closed form. The tensors are verified against direct numerical integration of the surface charges and with a finite element model, showing excellent agreement.

papers.title: How to calculate temperature and energy in Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulation of the dynamics of classical objects has become incredibly popular in natural sciences since the method was developed in the sixties. A conservative estimate is that it involves many hundreds of thousands of scientific articles and all subdisciplines of natural sciences. The earliest MD simulations also introduced a simple time-symmetric expression for the momentum and velocity, which has since been used uncritically in almost all MD simulations. The expression is incorrect and can lead to significant errors. But it is straightforward to replace the expression with the correct one, and the motive of the article is to draw attention to how to calculate velocity, kinetic energy, temperature, and energy in an MD simulation correctly. Newton's algorithm of the discrete dynamics has the same quality as his analytical dynamics, and Newton's discrete dynamics conserves the energy exactly. That is the second motive for the article, namely to show that conservation of energy in a conservative system is only obtained by the correct expressions for the velocity and kinetic energy.
